title: Why Don't Rally Cars Break When They Fly?
description:
A rally car can fly through the air for more than forty metres, land nose first on a gravel road, and keep going flat out to the next corner, as if nothing happened. Your road car would leave its wheels behind. The difference is not luck or magic. It is a list of parts built for the worst roads in the world. Today, ten parts of a rally car, and why each one exists.

Machine Reverse takes apart the machines you see every day and explains, part by part, why each one exists. This video covers 10 parts.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
1:12 1. The long suspension
2:36 2. The roll cage
4:06 3. The underbody shield
5:28 4. The mud flaps
6:44 5. The light pod
8:04 6. The roof scoop
9:22 7. The tall handbrake
10:31 8. The anti-lag system
11:51 9. The studded tyres
13:12 10. The pace notes
14:34 The verdict

Sources:
- Rally cars, roll cages, sump guards and mud flaps (FIA Appendix J): FIA, "Appendix J - Safety equipment" https://www.fia.com/regulation/category/123
- World Rally Car and Rally1 technical overview: Wikipedia, "World Rally Car" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Rally_Car
- Group B and the death of Henri Toivonen (1986 Tour de Corse): Wikipedia, "Group B" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_B
- Anti-lag system: Wikipedia, "Anti-lag system" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-lag_system
- Hydraulic handbrake and rally driving techniques: Wikipedia, "Rallying" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rallying
- Studded tyres at Rally Sweden: Wikipedia, "Rally Sweden" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rally_Sweden
- Pace notes: Wikipedia, "Pacenotes" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacenotes
